Few of us now leave the desk at lunchtime. A recent survey of 2,000 office workers in one region found that fewer than one in four take a proper break away from the screen, and nearly half admit to eating while answering messages. Many managers see this as dedication. I think it is a false economy. Studies of attention are consistent: after about ninety minutes of concentrated work, performance falls, and a real break, ideally outdoors, restores it. In a trial at a small design studio, staff who walked for twenty minutes at midday made around a third fewer errors in the afternoon than colleagues who stayed at their desks. Critics argue that a walk is a luxury when deadlines are tight. But the studio saw no drop in output: the walkers finished the same work in the same time, with fewer corrections. The real obstacle is cultural, because nobody wants to be the first to leave. Leaders therefore have to go first, and say openly that breaks are expected, not merely tolerated. Of course, a lunch walk will not fix an unrealistic workload, and it is no substitute for fair deadlines. But as a cheap, quick change it deserves a fairer trial in more workplaces than it gets.

Choosing a commuter bike usually comes down to two options, and each has real strengths. An electric bike gives a push on hills and in headwinds, so riders arrive faster and far less sweaty. This matters most on rides over ten kilometres. It also makes carrying shopping easy. On the other hand, it typically costs four or five times as much as an ordinary bike, it is heavy, often over twenty kilograms, so carrying it upstairs is hard, and the battery needs charging after about forty kilometres. Thieves also target electric models. An ordinary bike is cheaper, light enough to lift, and needs no charging. It is also simple to repair. However, hills are tiring, riders often arrive hot, and long trips can feel like a chore, which means some owners stop cycling in winter. Neither choice is correct for everyone. Weigh your distance, your hills and, importantly, where you will store the bike. The first electric bikes appeared in the 1890s, but only recently have batteries become light enough for them to be popular.

Good afternoon. People are often puzzled by the name, so let me start with what a heat pump does not do: it does not create heat by burning anything. Instead, it moves heat from one place to another. Even cold outdoor air contains some heat. A fluid called a refrigerant circulates in a sealed loop. In the evaporator, it absorbs heat from the outside air and turns into a gas. A compressor then squeezes that gas, which makes it much hotter. In the condenser, the hot gas passes its heat to the water in your radiators and turns back into a liquid. The cycle then repeats. It is the same principle as your fridge, only in reverse: a fridge moves heat out of the cold box and into the kitchen. Because the pump moves heat instead of making it, it is very efficient. For every unit of electricity it uses, it typically delivers about three units of heat. It keeps working in freezing weather, although it uses more electricity then. There are two caveats. The equipment costs more to install than a gas boiler, and it works best in a well-insulated home, where the heat stays inside.

I mention it only because stories like hers dominate the debate over short-term holiday lets, and they tell us little about what a city should do. Advocates of strict limits point to a clear pattern: neighbourhoods with many holiday lets have seen rents rise faster than elsewhere. The trouble is that this is a correlation. Popular districts attract both tourists and higher rents, so we cannot yet say which causes which. The best studies, which compare similar districts before and after new rules, suggest a real but modest effect, and one concentrated in a handful of central streets rather than across the whole city. This matters because blanket bans are sold as a way of returning homes to long-term tenants. Evidence from cities that have tried them is discouraging: many of the properties were sold, left empty or converted to other commercial uses, and few reappeared on the rental market. A ban can therefore remove a nuisance without delivering the benefit that justified it. None of this means that nothing should be done. A mandatory register of every listing would give the council data it currently lacks, and an annual cap on the number of nights a whole home can be let, set more tightly in the most affected streets, would target the problem where it exists. Such a system is harder to design than a ban, but it is likelier to achieve what voters actually want. Where hosts rent a spare room in their own home, the harm is much smaller and the rules should be lighter still.

In this randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 1,240 adults aged 40 to 74 with stage 1 hypertension received either a fixed low-dose combination of two antihypertensive agents or a placebo for twelve weeks. The primary outcome was the change in mean systolic blood pressure from baseline. At twelve weeks, mean systolic pressure fell by 9.4 mmHg more in the treatment group than in the placebo group (95% confidence interval 7.8 to 11.0). Dizziness was reported by 4.1% of participants receiving the combination and 1.8% of those receiving placebo; no serious adverse events were attributed to treatment. The authors caution that the follow-up period was short, that adults aged 75 and over and people with chronic kidney disease were excluded, and that the findings should not be extended to those groups. Longer trials are needed to establish whether the reduction is maintained and whether it lowers the risk of heart attack and stroke.

Here is where we stand. Overnight a pump failure at the Eastfield treatment works let some water bypass the final disinfection stage for about six hours. Of the fourteen samples we have tested from the Eastfield and Millbrook districts, two show traces of E. coli. Turbidity readings were also elevated, but those numbers mean little to the public. What does this mean? For most healthy adults the risk of becoming ill is low, and I want to say that plainly. But the risk is higher for babies, for older people, for pregnant women, and for anyone with a weakened immune system, so we are treating this seriously. Our advice is simple. Until further notice, residents in Eastfield and Millbrook should boil tap water for one full minute and let it cool before drinking it, using it for baby feeds, brushing teeth or making ice. Water for washing and flushing toilets is fine as it is. What we do not yet know is why the pump failed, or whether the two positive samples show a wider problem. Three options for the regional bus network were assessed. Option A, patching the existing network, would cost about 4 million a year and leave ridership flat. Roughly a third of the vehicles reach the end of their working life in 2029, and the replacement cost is not included in the figure. Option B, a core-frequency network, concentrates service on the twelve busiest routes, running buses every ten minutes. It requires 11 million of capital spending over three years. Modelling suggests an increase of 18% in passengers on core routes. To pay for it, six low-use rural routes would be replaced by an on-demand minibus service, which has been well received in the one town where it was tested but remains unproven at scale. Option C, a full redesign including new depots and traffic-priority lanes, would cost 24 million over five years and is projected to raise ridership by 30%. It would cause disruption on main roads for about three years. It depends on a state grant covering half of the cost; applications close on 30 September, and approval is not guaranteed. The consultation received 3,200 responses, with a majority favouring more frequent services. Officers' view is that Option B delivers most of the benefit at the lowest risk, and that it can be designed so that a move to Option C remains possible if the grant is awarded. The decision needed on Friday is whether to proceed with Option B and, separately, whether to submit the grant application for Option C before the deadline.
